The empty string `""` is not null.
exercises.solution:
`a?.Length` is null (because `a` is null), which interpolates as nothing: `[]`. `b?.Length` is 0. `a ?? "x"` is `x`. `b ?? "y"` is `b` itself, the empty string, because `??` only replaces null. Output:

```text
[] [0] [x] []
```

exercises.prompt: In a project with `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`, which statements are true? (Choose all that apply.)

options.label: Dereferencing a `string?` without checking it produces a compiler warning
options.feedback: Yes: warning CS8602, "Dereference of a possibly null reference".

options.label: Assigning null to a `string` variable throws an exception at run time
options.feedback: Not yet — nullable reference types add no run-time checks. The compiler warns; the program still stores the null.

options.label: `x!` tells the compiler to treat `x` as non-null, without any run-time check
options.feedback: Yes. The null-forgiving operator only silences the analysis.

options.label: `string?` compiles to a different run-time type from `string`
options.feedback: Not yet — that is true of `int?` (`Nullable<int>`), but for reference types `?` is only an annotation.

hints: Is the feature a compile-time analysis or a run-time check?
exercises.solution: True: (a) and (c). Nullable reference types are a compile-time analysis: they produce warnings (which you can make errors) and change nothing at run time. So (b) is false — the null is stored and the crash comes later — and (d) is false for reference types, though true for value types, where `int?` is the struct `Nullable<int>`.

answers: same ends | pair | ends big | one: 7
hints: Try the arms from top to bottom for each array.
`[var first, .., var last]` matches any array with at least two elements, but the `when` guard must also hold.
exercises.solution:
`[4, 1, 4]`: two or more elements with equal ends, so `same ends`. `[1, 2]`: the ends differ, so the guard fails and the next arm, exactly two elements, gives `pair`. `[1, 2, 300]`: ends differ, not a pair, last element above 100: `ends big`. `[7]`: one element: `one: 7`. Output:

```text
same ends | pair | ends big | one: 7
```

exercises.prompt: What happens if, in the lesson's `Fee` method, the arm `Card card => ...` is moved **above** the arm `Card { IsInternational: true } card => ...`?

options.label: The program compiles, and international cards are charged the domestic rate
options.feedback: Not yet — that is what would happen in many languages, but the C# compiler spots the problem first.

options.label: The program fails to compile, because the international arm can never be reached
options.feedback: Yes. Every international card is already matched by `Card card`, so the compiler reports that the later pattern has already been handled by a previous arm.

options.label: Nothing changes: the compiler sorts the arms from most to least specific
options.feedback: Not yet — arms are always tried in the order written; the compiler never reorders them.

options.label: The switch throws at run time for international cards
options.feedback: Not yet — international cards would match the general `Card` arm, if the program compiled at all.

hints: Switch expression arms are tried from top to bottom.
Can the compiler tell that one pattern includes another?
exercises.solution: The general `Card card` arm matches every `Card`, so a later `Card { IsInternational: true }` arm could never be chosen. The compiler detects this subsumption and reports an error (CS8510, "The pattern is unreachable. It has already been handled by a previous arm of the switch expression or it is impossible to match."). Put specific arms before general ones.

exercises.prompt: You write `public bool TryLoad(string id, out Order? order)`. Callers complain that after `if (TryLoad(id, out var o))` the compiler warns when they use `o.Total`. What is the best fix?

options.label: Tell callers to write `o!.Total`
options.feedback: Not yet — that silences the warning at every call site instead of fixing the cause once, and hides real mistakes.

options.label: Annotate the parameter: `[NotNullWhen(true)] out Order? order`
options.feedback: Yes. The attribute tells the null-state analysis that a true result means a non-null `order`, exactly like `Dictionary.TryGetValue`.

options.label: Change the parameter to `out Order order` and assign `null!` when loading fails
options.feedback: Not yet — this lies to the compiler: callers who ignore the `bool` would get a null typed as non-null.

options.label: Disable nullable warnings for the file
options.feedback: Not yet — that throws away the analysis for everything else in the file too.

hints: The method's contract is: true means found, false means not found.
The base class library expresses this contract with an attribute from `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis`.
exercises.solution: Add `[NotNullWhen(true)]` to the `out` parameter. The compiler then knows that inside `if (TryLoad(id, out var o))` the variable `o` is not null, and outside it may be. This is how `int.TryParse`, `Dictionary.TryGetValue` and the rest of the library are annotated.
